## What you will do

A **justice twin** is a language model asked to answer as one Justice of the
United States Supreme Court would, given passages from that Justice's own
opinions and a short description of a case the Court has not yet decided. The
Legal Digital Twins project runs nine such twins on every case of the October
2026 sitting and files their votes on FantasySCOTUS before the case is argued.
In this notebook you run one of those twins yourself, in about twenty-five
minutes:

1. **read the case:** the one-page packet the twin is asked about;
2. **meet the justice:** who the twin is, and the one number that summarises
   their voting record;
3. **open the evidence:** the eight passages retrieved from that Justice's own
   opinions, already found for you;
4. **assemble the prompt:** exactly what the model receives, line by line;
5. **ask the twin:** load the answer from the project's own run, or send the
   prompt yourself;
6. **sit the full bench:** nine twins, one predicted outcome, compared with what
   the Court actually did (practice case) or with the crowd (live case);
7. **change one thing** and see what moves.

Only Section 5 calls a language model, and only if an API key is set. Everything
else runs offline from the files beside this notebook.

**How to read this notebook.** As in Workshops 1 and 2, every table, text block
and figure the code prints has a number, given in bold just above the code that
prints it, and the text says which table, row or column a number comes from.

**Figure 1.0.** The whole machine. This notebook walks the middle row, for one
justice and one case, with the top row already built.

```{r pipeline-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "figures", "pipeline_map.png"))
```

The first block loads the packages the notebook uses and sets the folders it
reads from and writes to.

```{r libs}
library(data.table)
library(jsonlite)
library(ggplot2)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
OUT  <- file.path("..", "output")
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

---

## 1. The case

Two cases ship with the notebook. The **practice case** was argued in November
2025 and decided in June 2026, so we can check the twins against the Court. The
**live case** is argued on 5 October 2026 and will not be decided until next
year; the project's prediction for it was filed on 4 October. Start with the
practice case; Section 7 switches to the live one.

The block below loads the case index as `cases` and prints it.

**Table 1.1.** `cases`: the two cases in the package.

```{r cases}
cases <- fread(file.path(DATA, "cases.csv"))
cases[, .(slug, title, docket, term, argued, role)]
```

The twin never sees a brief, an opinion or a news story. It sees a **case
packet**: the question presented (verbatim from the Court), the lower court's
holding, the procedural posture and three arguments per side, assembled from the
public record before argument and checked by a person so that nothing in it
reveals an outcome. The next block sets `CASE`, loads that packet and prints it.
Change `CASE` to `"johnson"` for the live case.

**Text 1.1.** The case packet for `CASE`, as the twin receives it.

```{r packet, comment = ""}
CASE <- "landor"

packet <- paste(readLines(file.path(DATA, paste0(CASE, "_packet.md")), warn = FALSE),
                collapse = "\n")
cat(packet)
```

---

## 2. The justice

Each twin is one of the nine sitting Justices. The twin is told who it is, when
and by whom it was appointed, and one number: the Justice's **Martin–Quinn
score** for October Term 2024, a statistical summary of their voting record on a
scale where negative is liberal and positive is conservative. The score is a
coarse prior; the evidence in Section 3 is what the twin reasons from.

The block below loads the nine scores as `mq` and prints them in order.

**Table 2.1.** `mq`: Martin–Quinn posterior means for October Term 2024 (official
2024 release), with the 95% interval.

```{r mq}
mq <- fread(file.path(DATA, "mq_ot2024.csv"))
mq[, .(justice, post_mn, post_025, post_975)]
```

**Figure 2.1.** The same nine scores drawn as a line, so the spread is visible.

```{r mq-plot, fig.height = 2.8}
mq[, justice := factor(justice, levels = justice)]
ggplot(mq, aes(x = post_mn, y = 1, label = justice)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = post_025, xmax = post_975), width = 0, orientation = "y", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(angle = 45, hjust = -0.1, vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous("Martin–Quinn score, OT2024 (negative = liberal)") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL, limits = c(0.9, 1.4)) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The next block sets `JUSTICE` and loads everything the project prepared for that
Justice on this case: the evidence, the context blocks and the two prompt
messages. Change `JUSTICE` to any of the nine names in Table 2.1.

**Text 2.1.** Who the twin is.

```{r justice, comment = ""}
JUSTICE <- "kagan"

ev  <- fromJSON(file.path(DATA, paste0(CASE, "_evidence.json")), simplifyVector = FALSE)
tw  <- ev$justices[[JUSTICE]]
cat(sprintf("%s, %s, appointed by %s, on the Court since %d.\nMartin–Quinn OT2024: %+.2f\n",
            tw$name, tw$role, tw$appointed_by, tw$since, tw$mq_ot2024))
```

---

## 3. The evidence

The twin does not get the Justice's whole record. For each case it gets **eight
passages**, retrieved from an index of that Justice's own opinions (October Terms
1991 to 2024, about 37,000 passages across the nine) by three queries written
from the packet: the question presented, the doctrinal area and precedents, and
the two sides' first arguments. The retrieval has rules: at least two passages
from majority opinions and two from separate writings, at most two from any one
earlier case, nothing from the case at issue, nothing after October Term 2024.
The retrieval has already been done; the eight passages for `JUSTICE` on `CASE`
are in the file you loaded, together with a hash of the set so the run can be
reproduced.

The block below turns the eight passages into a table and prints where they come
from.

**Table 3.1.** `passages`: the eight passages retrieved for `JUSTICE` on `CASE`.

```{r passages}
passages <- rbindlist(lapply(tw$passages, function(p)
  data.table(n = p$n, case = p$title, term = p$term, type = p$doc_type, words = length(strsplit(p$text, "\\s+")[[1]]))))
passages
```

The next block prints one passage in full. Change `N` to read another. Ask
yourself the three questions the project's own spot-check asks: are these the
Justice's own words; is the case named the case the passage is about; does it
speak to the question presented?

**Text 3.1.** Passage `N`.

```{r one-passage, comment = ""}
N <- 1
p <- tw$passages[[N]]
cat(sprintf("[%d] %s (OT%d, %s)\n\n", p$n, p$title, p$term, gsub("_", " ", p$doc_type)))
cat(strwrap(p$text, width = 90), sep = "\n")
```

Each earlier case cited in the evidence comes with a **context block**: the
Reporter of Decisions' syllabus (prepared by the Reporter, not by the Justices)
and the Court's vote in that case from the Supreme Court Database, so the twin
knows what each earlier case was about and how it came out. The block below
prints the context for the first prior case.

**Text 3.2.** The context block for the first prior case cited.

```{r context, comment = ""}
ctx <- tw$context
cat(strwrap(ctx[[1]], width = 90), sep = "\n")
```

---

## 4. The prompt

The twin receives two messages. The **system message** says who it is, where its
evidence comes from, and that the case is undecided. The **user message** carries
the persona line, the eight passages with their context, the packet, and the task
with the JSON format of the answer. The project builds both from a template whose
hash is logged with every run; the text below is that build, exactly as sent.

The block below prints the system message.

**Text 4.1.** The system message.

```{r system, comment = ""}
cat(strwrap(tw$system, width = 90), sep = "\n")
```

The user message is long because it carries the evidence. The next block prints
its first sixty lines and its last thirty, which is where the persona and the
task sit; the middle is the evidence you read in Section 3.

**Text 4.2.** The user message, head and tail.

```{r user, comment = ""}
u <- strsplit(tw$user, "\n")[[1]]
cat(head(u, 60), sep = "\n")
cat("\n[...", length(u) - 90, "lines of evidence and packet omitted ...]\n\n")
cat(tail(u, 30), sep = "\n")
```

Notice three things. The twin is told the case has not been decided and to
disregard any recollection of an outcome. It is told the syllabus is the
Reporter's, not its own words. And it is asked for a probability, not just a
vote, so the bench in Section 6 can be read as more or less confident.

---

## 5. Ask the twin

The project's own answers were produced by Laurenz Günther's runs on the
project's model (Claude Opus 5.5, called as `claude-opus-5-5`, with the model id
the API returned recorded in the run log; adaptive thinking at medium effort,
temperature at the API default, 4,000 output tokens including thinking) and ship
with the package as a **cache**, so this section works with no key. If you
have a key in your `~/.Renviron` (see the setup email), the second block sends
the same prompt yourself.

The block below loads the cached answer for `JUSTICE` on `CASE` and prints it.

**Text 5.1.** The cached answer.

```{r cached, comment = ""}
cache_file <- file.path(DATA, "cached_answers.json")
ans <- NULL; cached <- NULL
if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache  <- fromJSON(cache_file, simplifyVector = FALSE)
  cached <- cache$cases[[CASE]]
  if (is.null(cached)) {
    cat("No cached answers for this case yet.\n")
  } else {
    # each case is bound to the index and prompt template of the run it came from; a mismatch with this
    # package's evidence file means the cached answer was produced from different inputs than those shown
    # above, and it is not used
    same_index  <- identical(cached$binding$chunks_sha256, ev$index$chunks_sha256)
    same_prompt <- identical(cached$binding$prompt_template_sha256, ev$prompt_template_sha256)
    same_input  <- identical(cached$inputs[[JUSTICE]]$retrieved_set_sha256, tw$retrieved_set_sha256)
    if (!same_index || !same_prompt || !same_input) {
      cached <- NULL
      cat("Cached answers for this case were produced with a different index, prompt template or evidence set",
          "than this package's evidence file; not shown.\n")
    } else {
      ans <- cached$answers[[JUSTICE]]
      cat("Model:", cached$model_id, " | index:", cached$binding$index_version, " | harness:", cached$binding$harness_version,
          " | run:", cached$run, "\n\n")
      cat(toJSON(ans, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))
    }
  }
} else {
  cat("Cached answers not yet in the package.")
}
```

The next block is the only one that calls a model. It reads your key and the
proxy address from the environment, sends the two messages, and parses the JSON
the twin returns. `MODEL` is the model the workshop proxy serves (`gpt-5-mini`);
the cached answer in Text 5.1 came from the project's model (Claude Opus 5.5) on
the same evidence and prompt, so a difference between the two is a difference
between models, not between inputs. That comparison is part of the exercise.

**Text 5.2.** Your own answer (runs only if `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set).

```{r live, comment = ""}
MODEL <- "gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"
key   <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")
base  <- Sys.getenv("OPENAI_BASE_URL", unset = "https://api.openai.com/v1")

ask_twin <- function(system, user, model = MODEL) {
  resp <- httr2::request(paste0(base, "/chat/completions")) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(key) |>
    httr2::req_body_json(list(model = model,   # gpt-5 models accept only the default temperature
                              messages = list(list(role = "system", content = system),
                                              list(role = "user",   content = user)))) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json()
  txt <- resp$choices[[1]]$message$content
  j   <- regmatches(txt, regexpr("\\{.*\\}", txt))
  fromJSON(j, simplifyVector = TRUE)
}

if (nzchar(key)) {
  mine <- ask_twin(tw$system, tw$user)
  cat(toJSON(mine, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE))
  writeLines(toJSON(mine, auto_unbox = TRUE), file.path(OUT, paste0("my_answer_", CASE, "_", JUSTICE, ".json")))
} else {
  mine <- NULL
  cat("No API key found; skipping the live call.")
}
```

---

## 6. The full bench

One twin is a guess; nine twins are a prediction. The block below assembles the
nine cached answers for `CASE` into one table: each Justice's vote (petitioner or
respondent), the probability it gave, and whether it expects to write separately.

**Table 6.1.** `bench`: the nine twins on `CASE`.

```{r bench}
if (!is.null(cached)) {
  bench <- rbindlist(lapply(names(cached$answers), function(j) {
    a <- cached$answers[[j]]
    data.table(justice = j, vote = a$vote, p_petitioner = round(a$p_petitioner, 2),
               disposition = a$disposition, separate = a$separate_writing)
  }))
  bench <- merge(bench, mq[, .(justice = as.character(justice), mq = post_mn)], by = "justice")
  setorder(bench, mq)
  bench
} else {
  cat("Cached answers not yet in the package.")
}
```

The next block turns Table 6.1 into the project's prediction: who wins, by what
split, and, for the practice case, how that compares with what the Court did.
For the live case it compares with the FantasySCOTUS crowd on 1 October instead.

**Table 6.2.** `verdict`: the twins' prediction next to the reference.

```{r verdict}
if (!is.null(cached)) {
  pet <- sum(bench$vote == "petitioner"); resp <- sum(bench$vote == "respondent")
  cat(sprintf("Twins: %s wins, %d-%d\n", ifelse(pet > resp, "petitioner", "respondent"), max(pet, resp), min(pet, resp)))
  if (CASE == "landor") {
    truth <- fread(file.path(DATA, "landor_outcome.csv"))
    cat(readLines(file.path(DATA, "landor_outcome_note.txt"), warn = FALSE), "\n")
    # the petitioner lost below, so 'respondent' = the Court's majority side when the Court affirmed
    verdict <- merge(bench[, .(justice, twin = vote)], truth[, .(justice, court = court_vote)], by = "justice")
    verdict[, court_side := ifelse(court == "majority", "respondent", "petitioner")]
    verdict[, agree := twin == court_side]
    verdict[order(match(justice, mq$justice))]
  } else {
    crowd <- fread(file.path(DATA, "johnson_crowd.csv"))
    cat(sprintf("FantasySCOTUS crowd on %s: %s %s\n", crowd$snapshot, crowd$crowd_outcome, crowd$crowd_split))
  }
}
```

The twins' accuracy per Justice on the practice case is the number of `TRUE` in
the `agree` column of Table 6.2 out of nine. One case tells you little; the
project's validation run scores the same twins on all 58 argued cases of October
Term 2025, and that number is on the slide behind you.

**Figure 6.1.** Each twin's probability for the petitioner against the Justice's
Martin–Quinn score. If the twins were only reading the score, this would be a
straight line.

```{r bench-plot, fig.height = 4}
if (!is.null(cached)) {
  ggplot(bench, aes(x = mq, y = p_petitioner, label = justice)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous("Martin–Quinn score, OT2024") +
    scale_y_continuous("Twin's probability that the petitioner wins", limits = c(0, 1)) +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

## 7. Change one thing

Everything above is one draw from one configuration. The question that matters
for the method is which inputs the answer depends on. Pick one of the three
changes below, re-run Section 5's live block, and compare.

**(a) Drop the score.** The block below removes the Martin–Quinn line from the
user message, so the twin has only the evidence and the packet.

```{r change-a}
user_no_mq <- sub("Ideal point \\(Martin–Quinn[^\n]*\n", "", tw$user)
nchar(tw$user) - nchar(user_no_mq)   # characters removed; about 260
```

**(b) Swap a passage.** The block below replaces passage `N` with a passage from
another Justice's evidence on the same case, keeping the header, so the twin is
reasoning partly from a colleague's words. (Your own choice of `OTHER` and `N`.)

```{r change-b}
OTHER <- "thomas"; N <- 3
other_p <- ev$justices[[OTHER]]$passages[[N]]
mine_p  <- tw$passages[[N]]
user_swapped <- sub(mine_p$text, other_p$text, tw$user, fixed = TRUE)
c(original = nchar(tw$user), swapped = nchar(user_swapped))
```

**(c) Another Justice, or the live case.** Set `JUSTICE` in Section 2 or `CASE`
in Section 1 and run the notebook again from the top; both load in a second.

To re-ask with a changed message, call `ask_twin(tw$system, user_no_mq)` or
`ask_twin(tw$system, user_swapped)` in the console, with a key set. Write down
what changed in the vote and the probability; that is the result of this
exercise, and it is yours.

---

## 8. What a twin cannot know

Three things to carry out of the room.

The twin only ever sees what is in Sections 1 to 4. Nothing from the term being
predicted is in its evidence; the case at issue is excluded from retrieval by
rule; the packet is checked by a person for anything that reveals an outcome.
When the twins are right, it is for reasons you can read; when they are wrong,
you can see what they were reading.

A prediction filed before argument is a prediction. The project's October votes
were filed on FantasySCOTUS on 4 October, each run logged with the hash of its
packet, its evidence set, its prompt template and its model. The decisions come
in the spring. Until then the numbers on the slide are the validation run on last
term's cases, where the answers are known, and nothing else.

And the obvious caveat: a model that has read the whole internet may remember a
decided case however firmly it is told not to. That is exactly why the record is
built on cases that are not yet decided.
